items.title: 11 Years, One White House Visit: Inside Xi Jinping's High-Stakes Trip to Washington
items.body:
## A Rare Trip to Washington

Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to arrive at the White House on September 24, marking his first visit to Washington in more than a decade. The trip, long anticipated by diplomats and trade analysts on both sides of the Pacific, comes at a moment when the world's two largest economies are trying to steady a relationship that has swung between cautious cooperation and open confrontation over tariffs, technology restrictions, and regional security.

For a leader who has traveled extensively across Asia, the Middle East, and Europe during his time in office, the gap in visits to the U.S. capital is notable. The last time Xi set foot in the White House was under a previous American administration, long before the trade wars, export controls, and pandemic-era disruptions reshaped the contours of the U.S.-China relationship. That history alone has turned this single visit into a closely watched barometer of where the two powers stand today.

## A Delegation Built for Business

Xi is expected to be accompanied by a large delegation that reportedly includes senior officials alongside executives from major Chinese corporations spanning manufacturing, technology, and energy sectors. The scale of the business contingent suggests Beijing wants the visit to be remembered not just for diplomatic photo opportunities, but for tangible commercial outcomes — potential agreements on trade volumes, investment commitments, or easing of restrictions that have squeezed companies on both sides.

Analysts following the run-up to the summit say the presence of so many corporate leaders signals that economic stabilization, rather than any single breakthrough, is likely to be the practical goal. Years of tariff escalation, supply-chain rerouting, and tit-for-tat export controls on items like semiconductors and rare earth materials have left businesses on both sides eager for predictability, even if a full resolution of underlying disputes remains distant.

## Taiwan Arms Sales: The Summit's Fault Line

Even as preparations move forward, the visit is shadowed by a familiar irritant in U.S.-China relations: arms sales to Taiwan. Beijing has issued pointed warnings that any new American weapons package for Taipei announced around the time of the visit could jeopardize the summit's tone, if not its substance. Chinese officials have long treated U.S. arms sales to the self-governed island as a direct challenge to what they consider a core sovereignty issue, and past sales have reliably triggered diplomatic protests, military posturing near the Taiwan Strait, and temporary freezes in bilateral communication.

Washington, for its part, has maintained that support for Taiwan's self-defense capabilities is consistent with longstanding U.S. policy and is not intended as a provocation timed to the visit. Still, the overlap between the summit and any pending Taiwan-related announcements creates a narrow window in which a single decision in Washington could ripple through the entire diplomatic agenda in ways neither side fully controls.

## What Success — or Failure — Could Look Like

For the Trump administration, a smooth visit offers a chance to project stability on the world stage and demonstrate that engagement with Beijing can coexist with a tougher trade posture. For Xi, appearing in Washington after such a long absence carries its own domestic and international signaling value, presenting China as a confident, indispensable partner in global commerce rather than an isolated rival.

Both governments have incentives to avoid a public rupture. A collapsed or acrimonious summit would rattle markets already sensitive to trade policy headlines and could undercut months of lower-profile diplomatic groundwork. At the same time, neither side appears willing to make major concessions on the issues that matter most to it — Taiwan for Beijing, and technology and trade imbalances for Washington.

## What to Watch in the Coming Days

As the September 24 date approaches, attention will likely center on a few key signals: whether any Taiwan arms package is formally announced before or during the visit, what specific economic commitments emerge from meetings between the business delegation and American counterparts, and whether the two leaders issue any joint statement addressing the broader trajectory of the relationship.

Given the fragility of U.S.-China ties in recent years, even a summit that produces modest, incremental outcomes — rather than a dramatic breakthrough — would likely be viewed by observers as a meaningful step toward reducing the risk of miscalculation between the two powers. Whether this visit becomes a turning point or simply a pause before the next flashpoint may not be clear until well after the delegations have gone home.

items.title: Two Straits, One Chokehold: How the Houthis Took Control of the Bab el-Mandeb Shipping Lane
items.body:
## A Week That Redrew the Red Sea's Map

In the span of little more than a week, Iran-aligned Houthi forces have completed a rapid military campaign that leaves them in effective control of the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow waterway that funnels shipping between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, and onward to the Suez Canal.

The offensive began on September 3 with a push to sever the road linking the city of Taiz to the port of Mokha. Within days, Houthi units had taken Mokha, the town of Dhubab, and the strategically placed island of Mayyun near the strait's mouth. Government forces then withdrew from Perim Island, the outpost that splits Bab el-Mandeb into its two navigable channels, handing the Houthis command of both passages. The group went on to seize the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands further north, rounding out its hold on the strait's key waypoints.

## Why the Strait Matters

Bab el-Mandeb is one of the world's most consequential maritime chokepoints, carrying a significant share of the traffic that would otherwise transit the Suez Canal, including a large volume of Gulf oil exports bound for Europe and beyond. Control of the strait's Yemeni shoreline gives the Houthis — and by extension their backers in Tehran — leverage over shipping lanes that Red Sea nations and global carriers depend on.

Analysts have noted the timing is especially pointed: the gains come as Iran maintains pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, the passage on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil moves. Together, the two chokepoints give Iran-aligned forces influence over maritime routes on both flanks of the peninsula, a development that has unsettled energy markets and regional governments alike.

## Houthi Assurances, Regional Unease

A senior Houthi politburo official sought to reassure international shipping firms and regional governments, saying the group poses "no danger" to Red Sea cargo traffic and that "freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly." Neighboring states and shipping insurers have so far treated those assurances cautiously, watching for any disruption to transit through the corridor.

Houthi fighters are now reported to be positioned close to the African side of the strait, a reminder of how tightly the group now grips the chokepoint's approaches.

## The Human Cost

The campaign has come at a heavy price for Yemeni civilians. Aid officials say the week of fighting has left several hundred people dead and forced tens of thousands from their homes, with the UN's migration agency estimating roughly 46,000 people displaced by the violence. Humanitarian groups are appealing for access to affected coastal communities as the front lines shift.

## What Comes Next

For now, shipping and energy markets are watching closely rather than reacting sharply, as vessel movements through Bab el-Mandeb continue despite the change in territorial control. But the durability of the Houthis' assurances, the response from Gulf states and Western navies, and the broader trajectory of the wider regional conflict will likely determine whether this becomes a lasting shift in who holds leverage over one of the planet's busiest trade arteries — or the opening chapter of a longer struggle for the Red Sea's southern gate.

items.title: 13th in Reading, 27th in Math: What America's Worst PISA Scores in Two Decades Really Mean
items.body:
## A Sobering Report Card for American Teens

Every three years, hundreds of thousands of 15-year-olds around the world sit down for the Programme for International Student Assessment, or PISA — a standardized test run by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that compares how students in dozens of countries perform in reading, math, and science.

The latest round of results has landed with a thud in US education circles. American teenagers posted a reading rank of 13th and a math rank of 27th among participating education systems, according to the newest data — scores that put the country at or near its lowest standing in more than twenty years of testing. For a nation that has long framed itself as a global leader in innovation and higher education, the numbers have reignited a familiar but increasingly urgent question: what's going wrong in K-12 classrooms?

## Reading Holds Up Better Than Math

The split between the two subjects is telling. A 13th-place reading rank isn't a disaster on its own — many countries cluster tightly in the middle of the pack, and small score differences can shuffle rankings significantly. Math is a different story. A 27th-place finish places the US behind most other advanced economies and well below the OECD average, continuing a slide that predates the pandemic but appears to have accelerated sharply in recent years.

Education researchers point to a mix of contributing factors rather than a single cause:

- **Pandemic-era disruption.** Extended remote and hybrid learning during 2020 and 2021 is widely believed to have interrupted the steady, sequential skill-building that math in particular requires.
- **Chronic absenteeism.** Attendance data in many districts has not fully recovered to pre-pandemic levels, and missed classroom time compounds quickly in math, where each concept builds on the last.
- **Uneven recovery efforts.** Federal relief funding aimed at academic recovery has largely expired, and results have varied widely by state and district, suggesting no single intervention has closed the gap nationally.
- **Widening gaps between students.** Multiple assessments, including domestic tests like the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), have shown that lower-performing students fell further behind during this period, which can drag down national averages even when top performers hold steady.

## Why Economists Are Paying Attention

PISA scores aren't just a matter of academic pride. Economists who study human capital have long argued that a country's long-run productivity and competitiveness track closely with the math and problem-solving skills of its workforce. As industries increasingly lean on data analysis, automation, and technical trades, a generation entering the workforce with weaker quantitative foundations could face a harder time filling — or being prepared for — higher-skilled, higher-wage jobs.

Business groups and workforce-development organizations have flagged this concern in recent years, noting that employers already report difficulty finding applicants with adequate math and technical readiness for skilled roles, from manufacturing to healthcare technology. A prolonged dip in foundational math skills, some economists caution, could show up years from now as a drag on productivity growth rather than an immediate crisis.

## A Familiar Debate, With New Urgency

The results have renewed a long-running debate among educators, parents, and policymakers over how to respond. Some argue for doubling down on high-dosage tutoring programs, which have shown promise in randomized studies for accelerating math recovery. Others point to curriculum standards, teacher shortages in STEM subjects, and the growing presence of smartphones and social media in classrooms as areas needing attention. There is broad agreement on at least one point: there is no single fix, and any recovery will likely take years, not one school cycle, to materialize in test scores.

It's also worth noting that the US has never topped PISA rankings, even in stronger years — a mix of income inequality, decentralized school funding, and demographic diversity has long made direct comparisons with smaller, more centralized education systems tricky. Still, the direction of the trend, rather than the absolute rank, is what has caught the attention of researchers: a consistent decline over multiple testing cycles is harder to dismiss as noise.

## What Happens Next

Expect the new scores to feature heavily in state and local budget debates over the next school year, as districts weigh how to allocate shrinking pandemic-relief dollars toward tutoring, literacy coaching, and math intervention programs. Parents may also see more schools experimenting with phone-free classroom policies and revised math curricula aimed at rebuilding foundational skills earlier.

For now, the PISA results serve as a data point rather than a verdict — a reminder that the pandemic's effects on education are still working their way through the system, and that closing the gap will likely require sustained attention well beyond the next test cycle in three years.
